These two patterns carry attitude: surprise, doubt, politeness or a hidden 'but'.
Rise-fall ↗↘ = strong feeling, surprise.
Fall-rise ↘↗ = doubt, politeness, 'yes, but…'
Rise-fall: real surprise.
Fall-rise: I am not convinced.
Fall-rise leaves it open.
The same tag question can mean two different things depending on whether your pitch rises or falls at the end.
Falling tag = I'm almost sure, just confirming.
Rising tag = I'm genuinely not sure, really asking.
I'm sure — just making conversation.
I'm genuinely unsure — please confirm.
Confirming what I already believe.
'Or' questions change meaning completely depending on the final pitch movement.
Rising on the last option = yes/no question about both together.
Falling on the last option = choose one of the two.
Choose one: tea, or coffee.
Asks: do you want a drink at all (either one)?
Exclamations use a big pitch jump to show strong feeling — surprise, excitement or admiration.
Every item in a list rises except the last one, which falls to show the list is finished.
Repeating part of what someone said, with a sharp rise, shows surprise or disbelief.
A gentle fall-rise on a request sounds more polite and less like a demand.
Offering two or more options in a sentence uses rise-then-fall, just like a two-item list.
A rising or level pitch on a statement (instead of falling) signals you're not fully sure.
A warm, falling intonation on greetings sounds friendly and confident.
Rising here sounds casual and friendly, not like a real question.
Sarcastic tone usually exaggerates the pitch and stretches the stressed word longer than normal.
The word 'great' is stretched and falls hard — the opposite of sincere.
A wide pitch range signals good news; a narrower, lower range signals bad news.
A long spoken answer should still fall clearly at the very end of each main idea, even with several sentences.
A statement with rising intonation can become a genuine question without changing the word order at all.
Each group of digits rises slightly except the very last group, which falls to show you've finished.
Warnings often use a sharp rise-fall on the danger word to grab attention immediately.
A calm, gently falling pitch with a soft final tone sounds comforting and reassuring.
Soft, gentle fall — not sharp.
Genuine compliments use a warm rise-fall to sound sincere rather than flat or sarcastic.
Ending a conversation politely uses a gentle, falling, friendly tone.
Negotiating uses fall-rise a lot — firm but leaving room for discussion.
Teaching intonation rises slightly at the end of each step to show 'more is coming' and falls on the last step.
Identical words can be a plain statement or a real question — only the pitch tells you which.
Sincere apologies fall gently and slowly — a flat or fast fall can sound insincere.
The exact same words can sound excited or bored depending only on pitch range and speed.
Formal announcements use clear, wide falls on each main point to sound authoritative and easy to follow.
A slight rise or level pitch in the middle of a sentence signals 'I'm not finished yet.'
Checking understanding uses a rising tag or a rising echo to invite confirmation.
Offers of help usually rise gently, sounding open and inviting rather than pushy.
Disappointment often uses a falling pitch that starts lower than usual and drops further, sounding flat and deflated.
Instructions fall clearly at the end of each command so the listener knows exactly when one instruction ends.
The pitch rises and the pace quickens as a story builds tension, then falls sharply at the climax.
Confusion often uses a rising, questioning tone even on statements, with a slight pause before.
Disagreeing politely often starts with a fall-rise to soften it before the falling main point.
A formal, careful list uses clear rises on each item; a casual list runs the items together more.
A gentle fall-rise softens a correction so it doesn't sound like an attack.
A toast uses a warm, rising build-up followed by a strong, confident fall on the final wish.
Relief often starts high and falls with a long, relaxed glide, almost like a sigh.
A formal introduction falls in a measured, even way; a casual one is faster with a friendlier rise.
Encouragement uses an energetic rise-fall to sound genuinely supportive.
Confident interview answers fall clearly and firmly at the end of each key point.
A slight rise or pause before 'however' or 'but' signals a contrast is coming.
Asking permission almost always rises to sound open and non-demanding.
Gentle bad news uses a soft, slow fall — a sudden hard fall can sound cold or blunt.
A flat, narrow pitch with little movement signals 'I don't really care either way.'
Prices fall clearly on the final amount to sound definite and easy to note down.
Calling someone's name to get attention uses a wide rise-fall so it carries and stands out.
A countdown rises with anticipation on each number and falls sharply on the final word.
A closing mixed set — decide falling, rising, rise-fall or fall-rise for each line before checking.
